nodes.name: Variety X
nodes.statement: To introduce the problem, let $X$ be an $m$-dimensional integral projective variety in $\mathbb P^n$.

nodes.name: Integer s (no hypersurface of degree < s)
nodes.statement: Let $s$ be an integer with the property that $X$ is not contained in any hypersurface of degree strictly smaller than $s$, i.e., $h^0(\mathcal I_X(s-1))=0$.

nodes.name: Minimal degree question
nodes.statement: What is the minimal degree that such an $X$ may have?
nodes.statement_short: Minimal degree of a variety not lying on any hypersurface of degree < s.
nodes.label: mindeg

nodes.name: Maximal number of degree-s hypersurfaces question
nodes.statement: For such a projective variety $X$, how big $h^0(\mathcal I_X(s))$ may be?
nodes.statement_short: How large can h^0(I_X(s)) be for such X?
nodes.label: maxnumb

nodes.name: Park's problem
nodes.statement: Park \cite[Problem A]{park} posed the problem of determining the maximal possible values of $h^0(\mathcal I_X(s))$, for every $s$ without further assumptions; thus our Question \ref{maxnumb} is more restrictive but different, inasmuch as we require the integer $s$ to be the minimal such that $h^0(\mathcal I_X(s))\neq 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Park's problem: determine the maximal possible h^0(I_X(s)) for every s.

nodes.name: Almost-minimal degree variety
nodes.statement: Furthermore, Park's extremal cases are related to the study of varieties $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ of almost-minimal degree, i.e., $\deg(X)=\textnormal{codim}(X)+2$; see \cite{bs, fu, park1, hsv}.

nodes.name: Collection A(n,s,m)
nodes.statement: Let $m \ge 1$, $s\ge 3$ and $n\ge m+2$. Define \[ \enm{\cal{A}} (n,s,m) = \left\lbrace \mbox{integral $m$-dimensional } X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n \ | \ h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0 \right\rbrace. \]
nodes.statement_short: Integral m-dimensional varieties in P^n lying on no hypersurface of degree s-1.

nodes.name: Elements of A(n,s,m) are non-degenerate
nodes.statement: Since $s>1$, any $X\in \enm{\cal{A}} (n,s,m)$ is non-degenerate, i.e., it spans the ambient projective space, as one clearly has $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}}_X(1)) = 0$.

nodes.name: Invariants d_{n,s,m} and alpha(n,s,m)
nodes.statement: We introduce two numerical invariants: \[ d_{n,s,m} = \min \left\lbrace \deg(X) \ | \ X\in \enm{\cal{A}} (n,s,m) \right\rbrace, \mbox{ and } \] \[ \alpha (n,s,m) = \max \left\lbrace h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) \ | \ X\in \enm{\cal{A}}(n,s,m) \right\rbrace. \] Hence $\alpha(n,s,m)$ is the maximal number, over the set $\enm{\cal{A}}(n,s,m)$, of the linearly independent hypersurfaces of degree $s$ vanishing on some $X\in \enm{\cal{A}}(n,s,m)$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimal degree and maximal h^0(I_X(s)) over the collection A(n,s,m).

nodes.name: Monotonicity of minimal degrees via cones
nodes.statement: For $m\ge 2$, we have $d_{n,s,m} \le d_{n-1,s, m-1}$. To see this, take $X\subset \mathbb P^{n-1}$ of dimension $m-1$ with minimal degree $\deg(X)=d_{n-1,s,m-1}$. Let $C(X)$ be the cone over $X$ with a single point as vertex: this sits in $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$, it has dimension $m$ and degree $d_{n-1,s,m-1}$. Moreover, it is clear that $C(X)\in \enm{\cal{A}}(n,s,m)$.
nodes.statement_short: d_{n,s,m} <= d_{n-1,s,m-1}, by taking the cone over a minimal-degree variety.

nodes.name: Arithmetic genus p_a(X)
nodes.statement: For a curve $X$, $p_a(X)$ denotes its arithmetic genus.

nodes.name: Curve notation A(n,s), d_{n,s}, alpha(n,s)
nodes.statement: For the ease of notation, we set \[ \enm{\cal{A}} (n,s):= \enm{\cal{A}} (n,s,1), d_{n,s}:= d_{n,s,1}, \mbox{ and } \alpha (n,s):= \alpha (n,s,1). \]

nodes.name: Family H(d,g;n)
nodes.statement: We introduce another piece of notation: \[ H(d,g;n) = \left\lbrace \mbox{smooth, connected, non-deg. } X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n, \deg(X) = d, p_a(X) = g\right\rbrace. \]
nodes.statement_short: Smooth connected non-degenerate curves in P^n of degree d and arithmetic genus g.

nodes.name: Family H(d,g;n)'
nodes.statement: In the range of degree $d\ge g+1$, define \[ H(d,g;n)' = \left\lbrace X\in H(d,g;n)\ | \ h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(1)) =0\right\rbrace. \]

nodes.name: H(d,g;n)' = H(d,g;n) for d > 2g-2
nodes.statement: Note that $H(d,g; n)'=H(d,g; n)$ whenever $d>2g-2$, as $\enm{\cal{O}}_X(1)$ is non-special.

nodes.name: Minimal degree of curves in A(n,s)
nodes.statement: The numerical invariant $d_{n,s}$ satisfies \[ d_{n,s} = \left\lceil \left(\binom{n+s-1}{n}-1\right)/(s-1)\right\rceil. \]
nodes.statement_short: The minimal degree of an integral curve in P^n on no degree-(s-1) hypersurface is ceil((binom(n+s-1,n)-1)/(s-1)).
nodes.label: i1

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.1
nodes.statement: Let \[ \delta = \left\lceil \left(\binom{n+s-1}{n}-1\right)/(s-1)\right\rceil. \] We show that $d_{n,s} = \delta$. For any integer $d\ge n$, the set $H(d,0;n)$ of all smooth and non-degenerate degree $d$ rational curves $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ has the structure of a smooth and integral algebraic variety, whose general point $X$ has {\it maximal rank}: hence $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t)) =0$ for some $t\in \enm{\mathbb{N}}$ if and only if $d t+1\geq h^0(\enm{\cal{O}}_{\enm{\mathbb{P}}^n}(t))$, i.e., whenever it is possible for the restriction morphism to be injective; see \cite{hi, be3}. Thus a general $X\in H(d,0;n)$ satisfies \[ h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0 \ \ \mbox{ if and only if } \ \ (s-1)d+1\ge \binom{n+s-1}{n}. \] This implies that $d_{n,s}\leq \delta$, as we have a (rational) integral curve of degree $\delta$. For the converse inequality, consider any integral curve $Y\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ such that $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _Y(s-1)) =0$, and let $k = \deg (Y)$. Since $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _Y(s-1)) =0$, we have $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _Y(s-1)) \ge \binom{n+s-1}{n}$. Since $Y$ is an integral curve (of arbitrary arithmetic genus), elementary considerations give \[ h^0(L) \le \deg (L)+1, \] for an arbitrary line bundle $L$ on $Y$. Thus \[ \deg(\enm{\cal{O}}_Y(s-1))+1 = (s-1)k+1 \ge h^0(\enm{\cal{O}}_Y(s-1))\geq \binom{n+s-1}{n}. \] Taking the minimum, the latter inequality implies $d_{n,s}\geq \delta$, which completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Upper bound from maximal-rank general rational curves; lower bound from h^0(L) <= deg L + 1 on integral curves.

nodes.name: Define delta
nodes.statement: Let \[ \delta = \left\lceil \left(\binom{n+s-1}{n}-1\right)/(s-1)\right\rceil. \] We show that $d_{n,s} = \delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce delta, the claimed value, and state the goal.

nodes.name: Maximal rank of rational curves
nodes.statement: For any integer $d\ge n$, the set $H(d,0;n)$ of all smooth and non-degenerate degree $d$ rational curves $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ has the structure of a smooth and integral algebraic variety, whose general point $X$ has {\it maximal rank}: hence $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t)) =0$ for some $t\in \enm{\mathbb{N}}$ if and only if $d t+1\geq h^0(\enm{\cal{O}}_{\enm{\mathbb{P}}^n}(t))$, i.e., whenever it is possible for the restriction morphism to be injective; see \cite{hi, be3}.
nodes.statement_short: Cite maximal rank of general smooth rational curves.

nodes.name: Upper bound
nodes.statement: Thus a general $X\in H(d,0;n)$ satisfies \[ h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0 \ \ \mbox{ if and only if } \ \ (s-1)d+1\ge \binom{n+s-1}{n}. \] This implies that $d_{n,s}\leq \delta$, as we have a (rational) integral curve of degree $\delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Deduce d_{n,s} <= delta from a general rational curve of degree delta.

nodes.name: Lower bound setup
nodes.statement: For the converse inequality, consider any integral curve $Y\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ such that $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _Y(s-1)) =0$, and let $k = \deg (Y)$. Since $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _Y(s-1)) =0$, we have $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _Y(s-1)) \ge \binom{n+s-1}{n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Take any integral curve Y in the collection; its sections of O_Y(s-1) are many.

nodes.name: Bound on sections
nodes.statement: Since $Y$ is an integral curve (of arbitrary arithmetic genus), elementary considerations give \[ h^0(L) \le \deg (L)+1, \] for an arbitrary line bundle $L$ on $Y$.
nodes.statement_short: Use h^0(L) <= deg L + 1 on an integral curve.

nodes.name: Conclude lower bound
nodes.statement: Thus \[ \deg(\enm{\cal{O}}_Y(s-1))+1 = (s-1)k+1 \ge h^0(\enm{\cal{O}}_Y(s-1))\geq \binom{n+s-1}{n}. \] Taking the minimum, the latter inequality implies $d_{n,s}\geq \delta$, which completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Combine to get (s-1)k+1 >= binom, hence d_{n,s} >= delta.

nodes.name: Arithmetic genus bound for minimal-degree curves
nodes.statement: Let $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ be an integral curve $X\in \enm{\cal{A}}(n,s)$ such that $\deg (X)=d_{n,s}$. Then its arithmetic genus satisfies \[ p_a(X) \le (s-1)d_{n,s}+1-\binom{n+s-1}{n}. \]
assumptions: $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ be an integral curve $X\in \enm{\cal{A}}(n,s)$ such that $\deg (X)=d_{n,s}$
nodes.label: i2

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.2
nodes.statement: Since $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$, Riemann-Roch shows that the statement is true if $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) =0$. Otherwise, assume $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) >0$. Since $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) \ge \binom{n+s-1}{n}$, Clifford's theorem gives $(s-1)d_{n,s} \ge 2\binom{n+s-1}{n}-2$. By Proposition \ref{i1}, we have \[ (s-1)(d_{n,s} -1)+2 \le \binom{n+s-1}{n}. \] Altogether, they give $\binom{n+s-1}{n}\le s-1$, contradicting the assumption $s\ge 3$.
nodes.statement_short: Riemann-Roch if h^1(O_X(s-1))=0; otherwise Clifford plus Proposition 3.1 give a contradiction with s>=3.

nodes.name: Non-special case
nodes.statement: Since $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$, Riemann-Roch shows that the statement is true if $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) =0$.
nodes.statement_short: If h^1(O_X(s-1))=0, Riemann-Roch gives the bound.

nodes.name: Special case via Clifford
nodes.statement: Otherwise, assume $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) >0$. Since $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) \ge \binom{n+s-1}{n}$, Clifford's theorem gives $(s-1)d_{n,s} \ge 2\binom{n+s-1}{n}-2$.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise apply Clifford's theorem.

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 3.1
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{i1}, we have \[ (s-1)(d_{n,s} -1)+2 \le \binom{n+s-1}{n}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 3.1 bounds d_{n,s}.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: Altogether, they give $\binom{n+s-1}{n}\le s-1$, contradicting the assumption $s\ge 3$.
nodes.statement_short: The two bounds contradict s >= 3.

nodes.name: Argument of Remark 3.3 (proof of Remark 3.4)
nodes.statement: Fix an integer $g$ such that $0\le g \le (s-1)d_{n,s}+1-\binom{n+s-1}{n}$. Again, as in the proof of Lemma \ref{i2}, Proposition \ref{i1} yields \[ (s-1)(d_{n,s} -1)+2 \le \binom{n+s-1}{n}, \] and so $g\le s-2$. \vspace{3mm} \begin{quote} {\it Claim.} We have $s-2 \le d_{n,s}-n$.\\ {\it Proof of the Claim.} By contradiction, assume $d_{n,s} \le n+s-3$. By Proposition \ref{i1}, in order to obtain a contradiction, it is enough to show \[ (s-1)(n+s-3) +2 \le \binom{n+s-1}{n}. \] Let $\varphi (n,s) = \binom{n+s-1}{n} - (s-1)(n+s-3)-2$. This function is non-negative in the desired range. Indeed, consider \[ \varphi (3,s) = (s+2)(s+1)s/6 -s(s-1)-2. \] It is clear this is non-negative for all $s\ge 3$. Moreover: \[ \varphi (n+1,s) -\varphi (n,s) =\binom{n+s-2}{n} -s+1 \ge 0, \ \ \mbox{ for all } \ \ s\ge 3, \] which leads to a contradiction. \end{quote} By the {\it Claim} and \cite{be2, be3}, a general curve $X\in H(d_{n,s},g;n)'$ has maximal rank. Moreover, for each integer $g$ with $0\le g\le (s-1)d_{n,s}+1-\binom{n+s-1}{n}$, there exists a curve $X\in H(d_{n,s},g;n)$ such that $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$. Since $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(1)) =0$, we have $h^0(\omega_X(-1)) = 0$. The latter condition is equivalent to $h^0(\omega_X(-t))=0$ for all $t\geq 1$. Hence $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t)) =0$ for $t=s-1,s$. Moreover, we have: \[ h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) = (s-1)d_{n,s}+1-g -\binom{n+s-1}{n}, \] \[ h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) = h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) +\binom{n+s}{n} -sd_{n,s}-1+g. \] Now, choose $g_0 = (s-1)d_{n,s} + 1 -\binom{n+s-1}{n}$, so that $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$. Furthermore \[ h^2(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-2)) =h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-2)) =0, \] where the right-most equality holds because $s\ge3$. By the well-known Castelnuovo-Mumford's Lemma, we derive \[h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t)) =0 \mbox{ for all } t\ge s. \] Finally, \[ h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) =\binom{n+s}{n} -sd_{n,s}-1+g_0 = \binom{n+s-1}{n-1}-d_{n,s}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Bound g by s-2, show d_{n,s}-n >= s-2, then take a general maximal-rank curve of genus g_0. Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity yields h^0(I_X(s)).
nodes.label: i3

nodes.name: s-2 <= d_{n,s}-n
nodes.statement: {\it Claim.} We have $s-2 \le d_{n,s}-n$.\\ {\it Proof of the Claim.} By contradiction, assume $d_{n,s} \le n+s-3$. By Proposition \ref{i1}, in order to obtain a contradiction, it is enough to show \[ (s-1)(n+s-3) +2 \le \binom{n+s-1}{n}. \] Let $\varphi (n,s) = \binom{n+s-1}{n} - (s-1)(n+s-3)-2$. This function is non-negative in the desired range. Indeed, consider \[ \varphi (3,s) = (s+2)(s+1)s/6 -s(s-1)-2. \] It is clear this is non-negative for all $s\ge 3$. Moreover: \[ \varphi (n+1,s) -\varphi (n,s) =\binom{n+s-2}{n} -s+1 \ge 0, \ \ \mbox{ for all } \ \ s\ge 3, \] which leads to a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: The minimal degree satisfies d_{n,s} >= n+s-2, by an induction on n of an explicit binomial inequality.

nodes.name: Assume the contrary
nodes.statement: {\it Proof of the Claim.} By contradiction, assume $d_{n,s} \le n+s-3$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume d_{n,s} <= n+s-3.

nodes.name: Reduce to inequality
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{i1}, in order to obtain a contradiction, it is enough to show \[ (s-1)(n+s-3) +2 \le \binom{n+s-1}{n}. \]
nodes.statement_short: By Proposition 3.1 it suffices to prove a binomial inequality.

nodes.name: Introduce phi
nodes.statement: Let $\varphi (n,s) = \binom{n+s-1}{n} - (s-1)(n+s-3)-2$. This function is non-negative in the desired range.
nodes.statement_short: Define phi(n,s) and claim it is non-negative.

nodes.name: Base case n=3
nodes.statement: Indeed, consider \[ \varphi (3,s) = (s+2)(s+1)s/6 -s(s-1)-2. \] It is clear this is non-negative for all $s\ge 3$.
nodes.statement_short: Check phi(3,s) >= 0.

nodes.name: Increment in n
nodes.statement: Moreover: \[ \varphi (n+1,s) -\varphi (n,s) =\binom{n+s-2}{n} -s+1 \ge 0, \ \ \mbox{ for all } \ \ s\ge 3, \] which leads to a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: phi increases in n, giving the contradiction.

nodes.name: Bound g <= s-2
nodes.statement: Fix an integer $g$ such that $0\le g \le (s-1)d_{n,s}+1-\binom{n+s-1}{n}$. Again, as in the proof of Lemma \ref{i2}, Proposition \ref{i1} yields \[ (s-1)(d_{n,s} -1)+2 \le \binom{n+s-1}{n}, \] and so $g\le s-2$.
nodes.statement_short: As in Lemma 3.2, Proposition 3.1 gives g <= s-2.

nodes.name: Maximal rank
nodes.statement: By the {\it Claim} and \cite{be2, be3}, a general curve $X\in H(d_{n,s},g;n)'$ has maximal rank.
nodes.statement_short: By the Claim and cited results, a general curve in H(d_{n,s},g;n)' has maximal rank.

nodes.name: Existence of curves
nodes.statement: Moreover, for each integer $g$ with $0\le g\le (s-1)d_{n,s}+1-\binom{n+s-1}{n}$, there exists a curve $X\in H(d_{n,s},g;n)$ such that $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$.
nodes.statement_short: For every admissible g there is such a curve with h^0(I_X(s-1))=0.

nodes.name: Vanishing of h^1
nodes.statement: Since $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(1)) =0$, we have $h^0(\omega_X(-1)) = 0$. The latter condition is equivalent to $h^0(\omega_X(-t))=0$ for all $t\geq 1$. Hence $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t)) =0$ for $t=s-1,s$.
nodes.statement_short: Non-speciality of O_X(1) propagates to O_X(t).

nodes.name: Cohomology formulas
nodes.statement: Moreover, we have: \[ h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) = (s-1)d_{n,s}+1-g -\binom{n+s-1}{n}, \] \[ h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) = h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) +\binom{n+s}{n} -sd_{n,s}-1+g. \]
nodes.statement_short: Riemann-Roch formulas for h^1(I_X(s-1)) and h^0(I_X(s)).

nodes.name: Choose g_0
nodes.statement: Now, choose $g_0 = (s-1)d_{n,s} + 1 -\binom{n+s-1}{n}$, so that $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose g_0 so that h^1(I_X(s-1))=0.

nodes.name: Castelnuovo-Mumford
nodes.statement: Furthermore \[ h^2(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-2)) =h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-2)) =0, \] where the right-most equality holds because $s\ge3$. By the well-known Castelnuovo-Mumford's Lemma, we derive \[h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t)) =0 \mbox{ for all } t\ge s. \]
nodes.statement_short: Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity gives h^1(I_X(t))=0 for t>=s.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Finally, \[ h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) =\binom{n+s}{n} -sd_{n,s}-1+g_0 = \binom{n+s-1}{n-1}-d_{n,s}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Compute h^0(I_X(s)) = binom(n+s-1,n-1) - d_{n,s}.

nodes.name: Summary of Remark 3.3
nodes.statement: Setting $g_0 = (s-1)d_{n,s} + 1 -\binom{n+s-1}{n}$, We have: \[ d_{n,s} \ge n+g_0; \] additionally, a general curve $X\in H(d,g_0;n)'$ satisfies \[ h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0 \mbox{ and } h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s))=\binom{n+s-1}{n-1} -d_{n,s}. \]
conclusions: a general curve $X\in H(d,g_0;n)'$ satisfies \[ h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0 \mbox{ and } h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s))=\binom{n+s-1}{n-1} -d_{n,s}. \]
nodes.statement_short: d_{n,s} >= n+g_0 and a general curve of genus g_0 has h^0(I_X(s)) = binom(n+s-1,n-1) - d_{n,s}.
nodes.label: observation

nodes.name: Value of alpha(n,s)
nodes.statement: Is it true that \[ \alpha (n,s) = \binom{n+s-1}{n-1} -d_{n,s}? \] Keep the definition of $g_0$ from Remark \ref{observation}. Does equality hold if and only if $X$ is a general curve in $H(d_{n,s}, g_0; n)'$?
nodes.statement_short: Is alpha(n,s) = binom(n+s-1,n-1) - d_{n,s}, attained exactly by general curves of genus g_0?
nodes.label: qw0

nodes.name: Formula for h^0(I_X(s))
nodes.statement: Let $n\ge 3$ and $s\ge3$. Let $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ be an integral and non-degenerate curve such that $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) = 0$. Fix a general hyperplane $H\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$. Then \begin{align} & h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) = \binom{n+s-1}{n-1}-\deg (X) -h^1(\enm{\cal{I}}_X(s-1)) + h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s))+ \\ & \nonumber \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ + h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) -h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s)). \end{align}
assumptions: $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ be an integral and non-degenerate curve such that $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) = 0$
nodes.statement_short: h^0(I_X(s)) expressed through the degree and h^1 of I_X and O_X in degrees s-1, s.
nodes.label: i00+

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.6
nodes.statement: Fix a general hyperplane $H\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$. Note that $h^0(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H}(s)) =\binom{n+s-1}{n-1}-\deg (X)+h^1(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H}(s))$. Since $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t)) =h^2(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t))$ for all $t\in \mathbb Z$, in order to conclude it is sufficient to use the long exact sequence in cohomology of the exact sequence \begin{equation} 0\to \enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)\to \enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)\to \enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(s)\to 0, \end{equation} along with the assumption $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$.
nodes.statement_short: Long exact cohomology sequence of the hyperplane restriction sequence (2).

nodes.name: Restriction exact sequence (2)
nodes.statement: 0\to \enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)\to \enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)\to \enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(s)\to 0,
nodes.label: eqi01

nodes.name: Hyperplane section
nodes.statement: Fix a general hyperplane $H\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$. Note that $h^0(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H}(s)) =\binom{n+s-1}{n-1}-\deg (X)+h^1(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H}(s))$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute h^0 of the hyperplane section's ideal.

nodes.name: Long exact sequence
nodes.statement: Since $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t)) =h^2(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t))$ for all $t\in \mathbb Z$, in order to conclude it is sufficient to use the long exact sequence in cohomology of the exact sequence \begin{equation} 0\to \enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)\to \enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)\to \enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(s)\to 0, \end{equation} along with the assumption $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude from the long exact sequence of (2).

nodes.name: Discussion of the terms of (1)
nodes.statement: In the setting of Lemma \ref{i00+}, as usual let $d = \deg (X)$ and $g = p_a(X)$. Since $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$, by Riemann-Roch, we have \[ h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) = (s-1)d +1-g-\binom{n+s-1}{n}. \] Define the numerical function $\psi (t) := h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t-1)) -h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t))$. For fixed integers $g$, $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s))$ and $\psi(s)$, the right-hand side of (\ref{eqi00+}) is a strictly decreasing function in $d$. Since $\deg (\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t)) =d+\deg (\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t-1))$, Serre duality and Riemann-Roch give \[ 0\le \psi (t) \le d. \] Therefore a class of curves for which the term $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) -h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s))$ is zero is realized when $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) =0$. Moreover, note that the long exact sequence in cohomology of (\ref{eqi01}) yields \[ h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) \le \binom{n+s-1}{n-1} -d, \] whenever $h^1(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(s)) =0$. As in \cite[Chapter 3]{szp}, let $\chi$ denote the minimal non-negative integer such that $h^1(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(\chi +1)) =0$. As classically shown by Castelnuovo, using (\ref{eqi01}) one obtains $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t)) =0$ for all $t\ge \chi$ \cite[Theorem 1, p. 52]{szp}. Furthermore, $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t)) \ge h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t+1))$ for all $t\ge \chi$ \cite[Lemma 2, p. 53]{szp}, and $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t))> h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t+1))$ whenever $t>\chi$ and $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t))\ne 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Riemann-Roch for h^1(I_X(s-1)), bounds 0 <= psi(t) <= d, and Castelnuovo's vanishing results via the invariant chi.
nodes.label: qw00

nodes.name: Minimal degree attained by smooth rational curves
nodes.statement: Note that the proof of Proposition \ref{i1} shows that a curve in $\mathcal A(n,s)$ of minimal degree $d_{n,s}$ can be chosen to be smooth (and rational).
conclusions: a curve in $\mathcal A(n,s)$ of minimal degree $d_{n,s}$ can be chosen to be smooth (and rational)

nodes.name: Curves of larger degree with h^0(I_X(s)) != 0
nodes.statement: Let $n\ge 3$, $s\ge 3$ and $d> d_{n,s}$. \begin{enumerate} \item[(i)] Is there an integral and non-degenerate curve $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ such that $\deg (X)=d$, $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$ and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s))\ne 0$? \item[(ii)] Can we choose such an $X$ to be smooth? \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: For d > d_{n,s}, is there an (smooth) integral curve of degree d on no degree-(s-1) but on some degree-s hypersurface?
nodes.label: xq1

nodes.name: Halphen's ranges for space curves
nodes.statement: Recall that, by Proposition \ref{i1}, \[ d_{3,s} = \left\lceil \left(\binom{s+2}{3}-1\right)/(s-1)\right\rceil. \] For $d, s\ge 3$, to each pair $(d,s)$, we attach the set of degree $d$ curves in $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^3$ {\it not} contained in any surface of degree $<s$. Given $(d,s)$, Halphen's question asks in particular to determine the maximum genus of a curve associated to this pair. It is customary to divide the set of pairs $(d,s)$ into four regions: \\ {\bf Range $\emptyset$}: $d < (s^2+4s+6)/6 $. In this range, there is no integral and non-degenerate curve $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^3$ such that $\deg (X)=d$ and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$ \cite[Theorem 3.3]{h0}, \cite{hh}. \vspace{5mm} {\bf Range A}: $(s^2+4s+6)/6 \le d < (s^2+4s+6)/3$. In this range, one finds curves with $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) =0$ and hence $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s))=0$. Thus if $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$ and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) \ne 0$, by Riemann-Roch one has $(s-1)d+1-g \ge \binom{s+2}{3}$ and $sd+1-g\le \binom{s+3}{3}$. Moreover, if $\lceil s(s+2)/4\rceil \le d <(s^2+4s+6)/3$, it is known such a curve exists for any such choice of $(d,s)$, along with curves reaching the maximal genera allowed; see, e.g., \cite{bbem, fl1,fl2}. To fill in all $(d,s)$ such that $(s^2+4s+6)/6\le d < \lceil s(s+2)/4\rceil$ the same result (the existence of curves with $(d,s)$ and $g= (s-1)d+1- \binom{s+2}{3}$) is only known for $s$ large enough, i.e., $s \geq 10.5\times 10^5$, by the recent \cite[Theorem 1]{be6}. \vspace{5mm} {\bf Range B}: $(s^2+4s+6)/3\le d < s(s-1)$. Hartshorne and Hirschowitz constructed, for any $(d, s)$ in this range, smooth space curves with very high genera and conjectured that they have the maximal genus for all curves associated to $(d,s)$ \cite{hh, ms}. \vspace{5mm} {\bf Range C}: $d>s(s-1)$. One finds a smooth degree $d$ space curve $X$ such that $\deg (X)=d$ and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$; Gruson and Peskine classified all such curves $X$ of maximal genus \cite{gp1}: if $d\equiv 0\pmod{s}$, these curves are complete intersections of a surface of degree $s$ and a surface of degree $d/s$; in all other cases $X$ is {\it linked} to a plane curve $C$ of degree $\deg(C) = s\lceil d/s\rceil -d$, by the complete intersection of a surface of degree $s$ and a surface of degree $\lceil d/s\rceil$. For $d\geq s^2$, we have $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) \le 2$ with equality if and only if $d=s^2$ and $X$ is the complete intersection of two surfaces of degree $s$.
nodes.origin_citation: Hartshorne 1980; Hartshorne-Hirschowitz 1988; Gruson-Peskine 1978; Ballico et al.
nodes.statement_short: Recalls the division of pairs (d,s) into Ranges empty, A, B, C and what is known on maximal genus in each.
nodes.label: x2

nodes.name: Halphen's question
nodes.statement: Given $(d,s)$, Halphen's question asks in particular to determine the maximum genus of a curve associated to this pair.

nodes.name: Range empty: no such curves
nodes.statement: {\bf Range $\emptyset$}: $d < (s^2+4s+6)/6 $. In this range, there is no integral and non-degenerate curve $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^3$ such that $\deg (X)=d$ and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$ \cite[Theorem 3.3]{h0}, \cite{hh}.
conclusions: there is no integral and non-degenerate curve $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^3$ such that $\deg (X)=d$ and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$

nodes.name: Existence of maximal genus curves in Range A
nodes.statement: Moreover, if $\lceil s(s+2)/4\rceil \le d <(s^2+4s+6)/3$, it is known such a curve exists for any such choice of $(d,s)$, along with curves reaching the maximal genera allowed; see, e.g., \cite{bbem, fl1,fl2}.
conclusions: such a curve exists for any such choice of $(d,s)$, along with curves reaching the maximal genera allowed

nodes.name: Ballico-Ellia: maximal genus in Range A for large s
nodes.statement: To fill in all $(d,s)$ such that $(s^2+4s+6)/6\le d < \lceil s(s+2)/4\rceil$ the same result (the existence of curves with $(d,s)$ and $g= (s-1)d+1- \binom{s+2}{3}$) is only known for $s$ large enough, i.e., $s \geq 10.5\times 10^5$, by the recent \cite[Theorem 1]{be6}.

nodes.name: Hartshorne-Hirschowitz maximal genus conjecture (Range B)
nodes.statement: Hartshorne and Hirschowitz constructed, for any $(d, s)$ in this range, smooth space curves with very high genera and conjectured that they have the maximal genus for all curves associated to $(d,s)$ \cite{hh, ms}.
conclusions: they have the maximal genus for all curves associated to $(d,s)$

nodes.name: Gruson-Peskine classification of maximal genus curves (Range C)
nodes.statement: One finds a smooth degree $d$ space curve $X$ such that $\deg (X)=d$ and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$; Gruson and Peskine classified all such curves $X$ of maximal genus \cite{gp1}: if $d\equiv 0\pmod{s}$, these curves are complete intersections of a surface of degree $s$ and a surface of degree $d/s$; in all other cases $X$ is {\it linked} to a plane curve $C$ of degree $\deg(C) = s\lceil d/s\rceil -d$, by the complete intersection of a surface of degree $s$ and a surface of degree $\lceil d/s\rceil$.
nodes.statement_short: Maximal genus curves in Range C are complete intersections (s | d) or linked to plane curves.

nodes.name: Known curves in Range A
nodes.statement: Assume $(d,s)$ is in {\bf Range A}. Let $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^3$ be any integral curve with $\deg (X)=d$, $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) =0$, $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$, and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) \ne 0$, i.e., by Riemann-Roch one has $(s-1)d+1-g\ge \binom{s+2}{3}$, and $sd+1-g\le \binom{s+3}{3}$, where $g = p_a(X)$ is the arithmetic genus of $X$. All curves constructed in \cite{bbem, be6, bef, fl1, fl2} have $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) = h^2(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$ and hence $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) =\binom{s+2}{2} - d$. The ones in the main results of \cite{bbem, be6} have $g= d(s-1)+1-\binom{s+2}{3}$, whereas the ones given in \cite[Proposition 4.3]{bbem} and in \cite{bef} have many different genera for the fixed pair $(d,s)$.
nodes.statement_short: Curves constructed in the literature in Range A have h^1(I_X(s-1))=0, hence h^0(I_X(s)) = binom(s+2,2)-d.
nodes.label: x3

nodes.name: Sets B(n,s,d) and B(n,s,d)'
nodes.statement: For all integers $n\geq 3$, $s\ge 2$ and $d\ge d_{n,s}$, let $\enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)$ (resp. $\enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)'$) denote the set of all smooth and connected (resp. integral) $X\in \enm{\cal{A}} (n,s)$ such that $\deg (X)=d$ and $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Smooth connected (resp. integral) curves in A(n,s) of degree d with h^1(O_X(s-1))=0.

nodes.name: Generalized Range A
nodes.statement: Curves in $\enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)$ are said to be in the {\it generalized} {\bf Range A}.

nodes.name: Genus bound in B(n,s,d)'
nodes.statement: Let $X\in \enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)'$. Since $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) =0$, Riemann-Roch gives $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) =d(s-1)+1-p_a(X)$. Since $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$, one obtains $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1))\geq h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _{\enm{\mathbb{P}}^n}(s-1)) =\binom{n+s-1}{n}$, and so: \[ p_a(X)\le d(s-1)+1-\binom{n+s-1}{n}. \]

nodes.name: Questions on generalized Range A
nodes.statement: We pose the following questions: \begin{enumerate} \item[(i)] For which choices of $d, s, n$, does there exist $X\in \enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)$ (or even $X\in \enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)'$) such that $p_a(X) =d(s-1)+1-\binom{n+s-1}{n}$? \item[(ii)] What is the maximal arithmetic genus of curves in $\enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)$ (or in $\enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)'$)? \item[(iii)] For which $g_0$ and every $0\le g \le g_0$, does there exist $X\in \enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)$ (or $X\in \enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)'$) with such arithmetic genus? \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Existence, maximal genus and genus spectrum of curves in B(n,s,d).
nodes.label: questiongeneralizedrangeA

nodes.name: Cohomology of extremal curves in B(n,s,d)'
nodes.statement: For any $X\in \enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)'$, one has $h^2(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$. Suppose there exists $X\in \enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)'$ such that $p_a(X) =d(s-1)+1-\binom{n+s-1}{n}$. Thus $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) = h^2(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$. By Riemann-Roch, $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1))=0$, and hence $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$. Therefore, these curves are exactly the integral and non-degenerate degree $d$ curves $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ such that $h^i(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$ for all $i\ge 0$; this is because for any curve $Y\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$, one has $h^i(\enm{\cal{I}}_Y(t)) =h^{i+1}(\enm{\cal{O}} _{\enm{\mathbb{P}}^n}(t))=0$ for all $i\ge 3, i\neq n$ and all $t\in \enm{\mathbb{Z}}$, and for all $t>-n$ when $i=n$. Take any hyperplane $H\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$. By the exact sequence (\ref{eqi01}), we have $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) = h^1(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(s))$. Assume $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-2))=0$, i.e., $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-2))=0$. Since $h^i(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t)) =0$ for all $i\ge 3$ and $t> -n$, we have $h^i(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1-i)) =0$ for all $i\ge 0$. In this case, Castelnuovo-Mumford's lemma gives $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t)) =0$ for all $t\ge s$: this implies that the homogeneous ideal of $X$ is generated by $\textnormal{H}^0(\mathcal I_X(s))$. Now we drop the assumption $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-2))=0$, and instead suppose $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) =0$, i.e., $h^1(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(s))=0$. This implies $d\le \binom{n+s-1}{n-1}$. In this case, the Castelnuovo-Mumford's lemma gives $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t)) =0$ for all $t>s$, which implies that the homogeneous ideal of $X$ is generated by $\textnormal{H}^0(\mathcal I_X(s))$ and $\textnormal{H}^0(\mathcal I_X(s+1))$.
nodes.statement_short: Extremal-genus curves in B(n,s,d)' have vanishing cohomology of I_X(s-1); Castelnuovo-Mumford gives generators of the ideal.

nodes.name: Numerical range where Question 3.8 has a positive answer
nodes.statement: Fix integers $n, d, g, s$ such that $n\ge 3$, $s\ge 3$, with \begin{enumerate} \item[(i)] $0 \le g \le d-n$, \item[(ii)] $(n+1)d \ge ng +n(n+1)$, \item[(iii)] $(s-1)d \ge \binom{n+s-1}{n} +g-1$, and \item[(iv)] $sd \le \binom{n+s-1}{n}+g-2$. \end{enumerate} By results shown in \cite{be2, be4, be5}, there exists a smooth, connected, and non-degenerate {\it maximal rank} curve $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ with $\deg (X) = d$, arithmetic genus $p_a(X)=g$, and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) =\binom{n+s}{n} -sd+g-1$. Hence, setting the arithmetic genus to be the maximal in this range, i.e., $g=d-n$, (i) and (ii) in Question \ref{xq1} have a positive answer, whenever \[ h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s))>0 \Longleftrightarrow (s-1)d < \binom{n+s}{n} -n-1. \] Note that inequality (iii) implies $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) = 0$, because $X$ has maximal rank.
nodes.statement_short: Using maximal rank curves, Question 3.8 (i),(ii) has a positive answer in an explicit numerical range.
nodes.label: numrangexq1true

nodes.name: Projective bundle construction of a minimal degree cone
nodes.statement: Let $m \ge 1$ and $e\ge 2$. Consider the rank $m+1$ vector bundle $\enm{\cal{E}} = \enm{\cal{O}} _{\enm{\mathbb{P}}^1}\oplus \enm{\cal{O}} _{\enm{\mathbb{P}}^1}(-e)^{\oplus m}$ on $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^1$. Define the corresponding projective bundle $T = \enm{\mathbb{P}}(\enm{\cal{E}})$ and let $\pi: T\to \enm{\mathbb{P}}^1$ be the vector bundle projection on $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^1$. The map $\pi$ makes $T$ a $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^{m}$-bundle and hence $\mathrm{Pic}(T) \cong \enm{\mathbb{Z}}^2$, with basis given by a fiber $f$ of $\pi$ and any line bundle on $T$ whose restriction to any fiber of $\pi$ has degree one; see, e.g., \cite[Ex. II.7.9]{h}. Among these generators we take the only one, say $h$, such that $|h| =\{h\}$ (this corresponds to the unique surjection $\enm{\cal{O}} _{\enm{\mathbb{P}}^1}\oplus \enm{\cal{O}} _{\enm{\mathbb{P}}^1}(-e)^{\oplus m} \to \enm{\cal{O}} _{\enm{\mathbb{P}}^1}$, \cite[Ch. II]{h}). As an abstract variety, $h$ is the trivial $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^{m-1}$-bundle over $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^1$ and hence $h\cong \enm{\mathbb{P}}^1\times \enm{\mathbb{P}}^{m-1}$. Similarly to the case of surfaces \cite[Ch. V]{h}, for any $a, b\in\enm{\mathbb{Z}}$ we have $|ah+bf|\ne\emptyset$ if and only if either $a=0$ and $b\ge 0$ or $a>0$ and $b\ge ae$. The line bundle $\enm{\cal{O}}_T(ah+bf)$ is globally generated (resp. ample) if and only if $a\ge 0$ and $b\ge ae$ (resp. $a>0$ and $b>ae$). The complete linear system $h+ef$ induces a morphism $u: T\to \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$, where $n = e+m$, as $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _{\enm{\mathbb{P}}^1}(e)\oplus \enm{\cal{O}} _{\enm{\mathbb{P}}^1}^{\oplus m}) =e+1+m$. Let $W= u(T)$ be the image of $T$. The morphism $u$ contracts $h$ to an $(m-1)$-dimensional linear space in $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^r$, whereas $u|_{T\setminus h}$ is an embedding. Thus $u$ is a morphism birational onto its image, as the support of $h$ is codimension-one. \\ \begin{quote} {\it Claim.} The variety $W$ has degree $e$. \\ {\it Proof of the Claim.} Since $u$ is a morphism birational onto its image, $\deg (W)= (h+ef)^{m+1}$, where the latter integer is the intersection product in the Chow ring of $T$ of $m+1$ copies of the divisor $h+ef$ defining the morphism. Since any two different fibers of $\pi$ are disjoint, the class $f^2$ in the Chow ring is zero. Thus $(h+ef)^{m+1} = h^{m+1} +(m+1)eh^mf$. Fix a fiber $F\in |f|$ of $\pi$. Since $h_{|F}$ is the degree one line bundle on $F$ and $F\cong \enm{\mathbb{P}}^{m}$, we have $h^{m}f =1$ and hence $(m+1)eh^{m}f =(m+1)e$. \\ If $m=1$, $T$ is a rational ruled surface. The normal bundle of $h$ has degree $h^2=-e$. Hence the conclusion follows for $m=1$. \\ Assume $m\ge 2$. Since $h \cong \enm{\mathbb{P}}^1\times \enm{\mathbb{P}}^{m-1}$, we have $\mathrm{Pic}(h)\cong \enm{\mathbb{Z}}^2$. As generators of the lattice $\mathrm{Pic}(h)$, we take the pullbacks of hyperplane classes of the factors through the projections $\pi _1: h\to \enm{\mathbb{P}}^1$ and $\pi _2: h\to \enm{\mathbb{P}}^{m-1}$, i.e., $\enm{\cal{O}} _h(1,0) = \pi _1^\ast (\enm{\cal{O}}_{\enm{\mathbb{P}}^1}(1))$ and $\enm{\cal{O}} _h(0,1) = \pi _2^\ast (\enm{\cal{O}} _{\enm{\mathbb{P}}^{m-1}}(1))$. \\ By definition, the restriction $h_{|h}$ is the normal bundle of $h$ in $T$ and hence $h_{|h} \cong \enm{\cal{O}} _h(-e,1)$, by induction on $m$ and using standard exact sequences on normal bundles. Thus $h^{m+1} = h^m|_{h} = -me$, concluding the proof. \end{quote} By this {\it Claim}, $W$ is a minimal degree $(m+1)$-dimensional subvariety of $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^{n}$, where $n=e+m$. It is a cone whose vertex is the $(m-1)$-dimensional linear space $V= u(h)$, and the base of the cone is a rational normal curve in any linear space $M\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ such that $\dim M = n-m = e$ and $M\cap V=\emptyset$. Thus $W$ is arithmetically Cohen-Macaulay. In particular, for any integer $s>0$, a divisor $X\subset W$ is contained in a degree $s$ hypersurface of $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ if and only if its pullback $X'$ to $T$ is a part of the linear system $|sh+sef|$, i.e., there exists a divisor $X''\ge 0$ such that $X'+X'' \in |sh+sef|$. Thus $X$ is not contained in any degree $s$ hypersurface of $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ if $X'\in |h+bf|$ for some integer $b \geq se+1$. In the Chow ring, we have: \[\deg (X) =X'\cdot (h+ef)^m = (h+bf)\cdot(h+ef)^m = \] \[ =h^{m+1}+meh^{m}f+b = b. \]

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.17
nodes.statement: Let $H\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ be a linear subspace with $\dim H = n-m$. Take a linear subspace $E\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ such that $\dim E =m-1$ and $E\cap H=\emptyset$. By \cite{hi, be2} (for the case $n=4$), \cite{be2} (for the case $n=5$) and \cite{be3} (for the case $n\ge 6$), there exists a smooth rational curve $Y\subset H$ such that \[ \deg (Y) =d_{n-m,s},\ \ h^0(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{Y,H}(s-1)) =0,\ \mbox{and} \ \ h^0(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{Y,H}(s)) = \binom{n+s-m}{n-m} -d_{n-m,s}. \] Let $W'$ be the cone with vertex $E$ and such a curve $Y\subset H$ as its base. Up to a projective transformation, the projective variety depends only on $Y$, and not on the choice of a linear space $E$ such that $E\cap H = \emptyset$. Consider the setting described in Remark \ref{ccc0} with $e =d_{n-m,s}$. Note that $W'$ is projectively equivalent to the $(m+1)$-dimensional minimal degree variety $W$ featured in Remark \ref{ccc0}. Let $X\subset W'$ be an integral divisor such that $X\in |h+df|$, upon an identification $W\cong W'$. Since $d\geq (s-1)d_{n-m,s}+1$, by Remark \ref{ccc0}, $X$ is not contained in any hypersurface of degree $s-1$. If $X$ were a cone, either its vertex is contained in $E$ or is a point on $Y$. In the first case, upon identification with $W$, as in Remark \ref{ccc0}, let $X'=u^{*}X$ be the pullback of $X$ through $u$. The image of $h\cap u^{*}X$ under the morphism $u$ would be a codimension-one linear space in $u(h)\cong E$. However, this is impossible, as the degree of $u(h\cap X)$ is $d-d_{n-m,s}>1$. The second case is not possible either, because the pullback $X'$ would contain the divisor $h$. However, $X'$ is integral because $u$ is an isomorphism outside $h$, and $X'$ cannot coincide with $h$, as $X$ is a divisor of $W$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a divisor in |h+df| on the cone over a minimal degree rational curve (Remark 3.16). Rule out being a cone by cases on the vertex.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.1
nodes.statement: Fix a general $C\in |\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s)|$. By Bertini's theorem, $C$ is a smooth and connected curve of degree $sd$. By the genus formula, $C$ has genus \[ g = 1 + (s^2d + \omega _X\cdot \enm{\cal{O}} _X(s))/2. \] Multiplying by the section $C$ yields the exact sequence \begin{equation} 0 \to \enm{\cal{O}} _X\to \enm{\cal{O}} _X(s)\to \enm{\cal{O}} _C(s)\to 0. \end{equation} Thus $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s)) \le h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _C(s)) +1$, where equality holds if $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X)=0$. \\ If $s^2d = \deg (\enm{\cal{O}} _C(s)) \le 2g-2$, then this divisor on $C$ is special and Clifford's theorem \cite[pp. 107--108]{acgh} gives \[ h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _C(s)) \le 1 +s^2d/2. \] Whence $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s))\le 2 +s^2d/2$. From now on, assume $s^2d\ge 2g-1$ (or equivalently, $\enm{\cal{O}} _C(s)$ is non-special). Again, by the genus formula, one has \[ \omega _X \cdot \enm{\cal{O}} _X(1) <0. \] Note that Riemann-Roch gives $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _C(s)) =s^2d +1-g = \frac{1}{2}(s^2d -s\omega _X\cdot \enm{\cal{O}} _X(1))$. Before we proceed, recall that a line bundle $\mathcal L$ on a projective variety $X$ of dimension $\ge 2$ is said to be \emph{nef} if $\mathcal L \cdot C\ge 0$, for every algebraic curve $C\subset X$. \begin{quote} {\it Claim.} If $\omega _X \cdot \enm{\cal{O}} _X(1) <0$, then $\kappa (X)=-\infty$. \\ {\it Proof of the Claim.} Assume on the contrary that $\kappa (X)\ge 0$. Let $X'$ be the minimal model of $X$ and $\varphi: X\to X'$ be the corresponding morphism. Since $\kappa (X') =\kappa (X)\ge 0$, $\omega _{X'}$ is nef. We have $\omega _X \cong \varphi^\ast\omega _{X'} +E$, where $E$ is an effective divisor and $E = 0$ if and only if $X$ is minimal. Since $\varphi^\ast\omega _{X'}$ is nef and $\enm{\cal{O}}_X(1)$ is effective, we derive \[ ( \varphi^\ast \omega _{X'} +E)\cdot \enm{\cal{O}} _X(1)\ge 0, \] which is a contradiction. \end{quote} The {\it Claim} shows that the Kodaira dimension of $X$ is $\kappa (X) = -\infty$, and statement (i) is proven. We recall the Kawamata Rationality Theorem in the case of smooth surfaces. Let $X$ be a smooth projective surface such that $\omega _X$ is {\it not} nef. For each ample line bundle $\enm{\cal{L}}$ on $X$, the {\it nef-value} $\tau$ of $\enm{\cal{L}}$ with respect to $\omega_X$ is defined as \[ \tau(\enm{\cal{L}}) = \sup \lbrace t>0 \ | \ \enm{\cal{L}} +t\omega _X \mbox{ is nef} \rbrace, \] where $\enm{\cal{L}} +t\omega _X$ is viewed as a functional on the cone of curves depending on a parameter $t$. The aforementioned theorem states that the real number $\tau$ is rational, $\tau = u/v$, where $u$ is a positive integer and $v\in \{1,2,3\}$; see, e.g., \cite[Theorem 1.5.2]{bs}, \cite[Corollary 1-2-15]{matsuki}. Moreover, $\enm{\cal{L}} +\tau \omega_X$ is nef \cite[Lemma 1.5.5]{bs}, \cite[Theorem 1-2-14]{matsuki}. Thus we have the following cases: \begin{itemize} \item $u=1$ and $v=3$. The cone of curves of $X$ has an {\it extremal ray} of {\it length} $3 =\dim X +1$; see \cite{matsuki} for these notions. This implies $X\cong \enm{\mathbb{P}}^2$ and $\enm{\cal{O}} _X(1)$ is the generator of $\mathrm{Pic}(X)$. Since $n\ge 4$, $X$ is embedded as described in the statement. \vspace{2mm} \item $u=1$ and $v=2$. Since $\enm{\cal{L}}+\frac{1}{2}\omega _X$ is nef, so is the line bundle $2\enm{\cal{L}}+\omega _X$. In this case, there exists a curve $C\subset X$ such that $C\cdot (2\enm{\cal{L}}+\omega _X) =0$. By \cite[Theorem 1-4-8]{matsuki}, $X$ is a $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^1$-bundle over a smooth curve $D$, $\pi: X\to D$, and $\enm{\cal{L}}\cong\enm{\cal{O}} _X(1)$ has degree $1$ on each fiber $C$ of $\pi$. In such a case, $\omega _X(2)$ is nef and hence $\omega_X\cdot \enm{\cal{O}}_X(1) \geq -2$. This proves statement (ii). \\ \vspace{2mm} \item $u\ge 2$ or $v=1$. Then $\omega _X^{\otimes 2}(3)$ is nef and therefore $\omega_X\cdot \enm{\cal{O}}_X(1)\geq -3/2$. In this case, we obtain (iv). \end{itemize} In conclusion, the discussion above yields $\omega_X\cdot \enm{\cal{O}}_X(1)\geq -3$ for all $X$, with equality if and only if $X\cong \enm{\mathbb{P}}^2$. This proves statement (iii).
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to a general curve C in |O_X(s)|: Clifford handles the special case; otherwise Kawamata rationality of the nef value gives omega_X.O_X(1) >= -3, -2 or -3/2 by case.

nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a smooth projective surface such that $\omega _X$ is {\it not} nef. For each ample line bundle $\enm{\cal{L}}$ on $X$, the {\it nef-value} $\tau$ of $\enm{\cal{L}}$ with respect to $\omega_X$ is defined as \[ \tau(\enm{\cal{L}}) = \sup \lbrace t>0 \ | \ \enm{\cal{L}} +t\omega _X \mbox{ is nef} \rbrace, \] where $\enm{\cal{L}} +t\omega _X$ is viewed as a functional on the cone of curves depending on a parameter $t$. The aforementioned theorem states that the real number $\tau$ is rational, $\tau = u/v$, where $u$ is a positive integer and $v\in \{1,2,3\}$; see, e.g., \cite[Theorem 1.5.2]{bs}, \cite[Corollary 1-2-15]{matsuki}. Moreover, $\enm{\cal{L}} +\tau \omega_X$ is nef \cite[Lemma 1.5.5]{bs}, \cite[Theorem 1-2-14]{matsuki}.
assumptions: $X$ be a smooth projective surface such that $\omega _X$ is {\it not} nef
conclusions: the real number $\tau$ is rational, $\tau = u/v$, where $u$ is a positive integer and $v\in \{1,2,3\}$
nodes.statement_short: The nef value of an ample line bundle on a smooth surface with non-nef canonical bundle is u/v with v in {1,2,3}.

nodes.name: General curve C
nodes.statement: Fix a general $C\in |\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s)|$. By Bertini's theorem, $C$ is a smooth and connected curve of degree $sd$. By the genus formula, $C$ has genus \[ g = 1 + (s^2d + \omega _X\cdot \enm{\cal{O}} _X(s))/2. \]
nodes.statement_short: Take a general smooth curve C in |O_X(s)| and compute its genus.

nodes.name: Restriction sequence
nodes.statement: Multiplying by the section $C$ yields the exact sequence \begin{equation} 0 \to \enm{\cal{O}} _X\to \enm{\cal{O}} _X(s)\to \enm{\cal{O}} _C(s)\to 0. \end{equation} Thus $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s)) \le h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _C(s)) +1$, where equality holds if $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: From the sequence (3), h^0(O_X(s)) <= h^0(O_C(s))+1.

nodes.name: Special case
nodes.statement: If $s^2d = \deg (\enm{\cal{O}} _C(s)) \le 2g-2$, then this divisor on $C$ is special and Clifford's theorem \cite[pp. 107--108]{acgh} gives \[ h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _C(s)) \le 1 +s^2d/2. \] Whence $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s))\le 2 +s^2d/2$.
nodes.statement_short: If O_C(s) is special, Clifford gives the bound of (i).

nodes.name: Non-special case
nodes.statement: From now on, assume $s^2d\ge 2g-1$ (or equivalently, $\enm{\cal{O}} _C(s)$ is non-special). Again, by the genus formula, one has \[ \omega _X \cdot \enm{\cal{O}} _X(1) <0. \] Note that Riemann-Roch gives $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _C(s)) =s^2d +1-g = \frac{1}{2}(s^2d -s\omega _X\cdot \enm{\cal{O}} _X(1))$. Before we proceed, recall that a line bundle $\mathcal L$ on a projective variety $X$ of dimension $\ge 2$ is said to be \emph{nef} if $\mathcal L \cdot C\ge 0$, for every algebraic curve $C\subset X$.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise omega_X.O_X(1) < 0; recall nefness.

nodes.name: Statement (i)
nodes.statement: The {\it Claim} shows that the Kodaira dimension of $X$ is $\kappa (X) = -\infty$, and statement (i) is proven.
nodes.statement_short: By the Claim kappa = -infinity, proving (i).

nodes.name: Recall Kawamata
nodes.statement: We recall the Kawamata Rationality Theorem in the case of smooth surfaces. Let $X$ be a smooth projective surface such that $\omega _X$ is {\it not} nef. For each ample line bundle $\enm{\cal{L}}$ on $X$, the {\it nef-value} $\tau$ of $\enm{\cal{L}}$ with respect to $\omega_X$ is defined as \[ \tau(\enm{\cal{L}}) = \sup \lbrace t>0 \ | \ \enm{\cal{L}} +t\omega _X \mbox{ is nef} \rbrace, \] where $\enm{\cal{L}} +t\omega _X$ is viewed as a functional on the cone of curves depending on a parameter $t$. The aforementioned theorem states that the real number $\tau$ is rational, $\tau = u/v$, where $u$ is a positive integer and $v\in \{1,2,3\}$; see, e.g., \cite[Theorem 1.5.2]{bs}, \cite[Corollary 1-2-15]{matsuki}. Moreover, $\enm{\cal{L}} +\tau \omega_X$ is nef \cite[Lemma 1.5.5]{bs}, \cite[Theorem 1-2-14]{matsuki}. Thus we have the following cases:
nodes.statement_short: Recall the Kawamata Rationality Theorem for the nef value tau = u/v.

nodes.name: Case u=1, v=3
nodes.statement: $u=1$ and $v=3$. The cone of curves of $X$ has an {\it extremal ray} of {\it length} $3 =\dim X +1$; see \cite{matsuki} for these notions. This implies $X\cong \enm{\mathbb{P}}^2$ and $\enm{\cal{O}} _X(1)$ is the generator of $\mathrm{Pic}(X)$. Since $n\ge 4$, $X$ is embedded as described in the statement.
nodes.statement_short: Extremal ray of length 3: X is P^2.

nodes.name: Case u=1, v=2
nodes.statement: $u=1$ and $v=2$. Since $\enm{\cal{L}}+\frac{1}{2}\omega _X$ is nef, so is the line bundle $2\enm{\cal{L}}+\omega _X$. In this case, there exists a curve $C\subset X$ such that $C\cdot (2\enm{\cal{L}}+\omega _X) =0$. By \cite[Theorem 1-4-8]{matsuki}, $X$ is a $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^1$-bundle over a smooth curve $D$, $\pi: X\to D$, and $\enm{\cal{L}}\cong\enm{\cal{O}} _X(1)$ has degree $1$ on each fiber $C$ of $\pi$. In such a case, $\omega _X(2)$ is nef and hence $\omega_X\cdot \enm{\cal{O}}_X(1) \geq -2$. This proves statement (ii).
nodes.statement_short: X is a P^1-bundle with degree-1 fibers; omega_X.O_X(1) >= -2, proving (ii).

nodes.name: Case u>=2 or v=1
nodes.statement: $u\ge 2$ or $v=1$. Then $\omega _X^{\otimes 2}(3)$ is nef and therefore $\omega_X\cdot \enm{\cal{O}}_X(1)\geq -3/2$. In this case, we obtain (iv).
nodes.statement_short: omega^2(3) nef gives (iv).

nodes.name: Statement (iii)
nodes.statement: In conclusion, the discussion above yields $\omega_X\cdot \enm{\cal{O}}_X(1)\geq -3$ for all $X$, with equality if and only if $X\cong \enm{\mathbb{P}}^2$. This proves statement (iii).
nodes.statement_short: omega_X.O_X(1) >= -3 with equality only for P^2, proving (iii).

nodes.name: Bound on d_{n,s+1,2} via Veronese projections
nodes.statement: Let $n, s$ be integers as in the assumptions of Theorem \ref{ma1}, and let $k$ be an integer. Assume $\binom{n+s}{n} \le 1+(s^2+3s)k^2/2$. From the ideal sheaf exact sequence and Theorem \ref{ma1} (iii), one has \[ h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) \ge 1+(s^2+3s)k^2/2 -\binom{n+s}{n}, \] for any isomorphic projection $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ of the degree $k$ Veronese embedding of $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^2$. Assuming the existence of such an $X$ with the additional property that the latter inequality is an equality, one obtains $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}}_X(s))=0$. Thus $d_{n,s+1,2} \le \deg(X) = k^2$.
nodes.statement_short: If a projected Veronese surface has the extremal h^1(I_X(s)), then d_{n,s+1,2} <= k^2.
nodes.label: ma2

nodes.name: Ballico-Ellia: quadrics through projected Veronese surfaces
nodes.statement: Let $d \ge 2$ and $n\ge 5$. Let $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ be a general isomorphic linear projection of a degree $k$ Veronese embedding $Y\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^N$ of $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^2$, where $N= (k^2+3k)/2$. Then \[ h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(2)) = \max \left\{0,\binom{n+2}{2} -\binom{2k+2}{2}\right\}, \] \[ \mbox{ and } h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(2)) = \max \left\{0,\binom{2k+2}{2}-\binom{n+2}{2} \right\}. \]
assumptions:
$X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ be a general isomorphic linear projection of
a degree $k$ Veronese embedding $Y\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^N$ of $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^2$, where $N= (k^2+3k)/2$
nodes.statement_short: General projections of Veronese surfaces have maximal rank for quadrics.
nodes.label: be1

nodes.name: Bound on d_{n,3,2} for odd n
nodes.statement: Let $n\ge 5$ be an odd integer. Then $d_{n,3,2} \le (n+1)^2/4$. \begin{proof} Let $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ be a general linear projection of the degree $(n+1)/2$ Veronese embedding of $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^2$. By Proposition \ref{be1}, we have \[ h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(2)) =\max \left\{0,\binom{n+2}{2} -\binom{n+3}{2}\right\}=0. \] \end{proof}
nodes.label: be3

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.4
nodes.statement: Let $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ be a general linear projection of the degree $(n+1)/2$ Veronese embedding of $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^2$. By Proposition \ref{be1}, we have \[ h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(2)) =\max \left\{0,\binom{n+2}{2} -\binom{n+3}{2}\right\}=0. \]
nodes.statement_short: Project the degree-(n+1)/2 Veronese surface; Proposition 4.3 gives no quadrics.

nodes.name: Maximal rank of projected Veronese surfaces in degree s
nodes.statement: Fix integers $d \ge 2, s\ge 3$, and $n\ge 5$. Let $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ be a general isomorphic linear projection of a degree $k$ Veronese embedding $Y\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^N$ of $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^2$, where $N= (k^2+3k)/2$. Is it true that \[ h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) = \max \left\{0,\binom{n+s}{n} -\binom{sk+2}{2}\right\}, \] \[ \mbox{ and } h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) = \max \left\{0,\binom{sk+2}{2}-\binom{n+s}{n} \right\}? \]
nodes.statement_short: Does Proposition 4.3 extend to hypersurfaces of degree s >= 3?

nodes.name: Quadrics through even-dimensional-ambient surfaces
nodes.statement: Let $n\ge 6$ be even. Then $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(2)) \ge \binom{n+2}{2} - 1 - 5d$ for all smooth connected and non-degenerate surfaces of degree $d$. Moreover, there exists a smooth and connected surface $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ such that $\deg (X) =n^2/4$, $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(2)) =0$, and $X\cong \enm{\mathbb{P}}^2$.
conclusions: $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(2)) \ge \binom{n+2}{2} - 1 - 5d$ for all smooth connected and non-degenerate surfaces of degree $d$
there exists a smooth and connected surface $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ such that $\deg (X) =n^2/4$, $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(2)) =0$, and $X\cong \enm{\mathbb{P}}^2$
$h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(2)) \ge \binom{n+2}{2} - 1 - 5d$ for all smooth connected and non-degenerate surfaces of degree $d$
there exists a smooth and connected surface $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ such that $\deg (X) =n^2/4$, $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(2)) =0$, and $X\cong \enm{\mathbb{P}}^2$

nodes.label: be2

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.6
nodes.statement: The first part is statement (iii) of Theorem \ref{ma1}. By Proposition \ref{be1}, the general isomorphic linear projection of the degree $k$ Veronese surface has \[ h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(2)) =\max \left\{0,\binom{n+2}{2} -\binom{2k+2}{2}\right\}. \] Thus the choice $k = n/2$ establishes the second statement.
nodes.statement_short: First part from Theorem 4.1(iii); second from Proposition 4.3 with k = n/2.

nodes.name: First part
nodes.statement: The first part is statement (iii) of Theorem \ref{ma1}.
nodes.statement_short: First part is Theorem 4.1(iii).

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 4.3
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{be1}, the general isomorphic linear projection of the degree $k$ Veronese surface has \[ h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(2)) =\max \left\{0,\binom{n+2}{2} -\binom{2k+2}{2}\right\}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Quadrics through projected Veronese surfaces.

nodes.name: Choose k
nodes.statement: Thus the choice $k = n/2$ establishes the second statement.
nodes.statement_short: Take k = n/2.

nodes.name: Quadric bound via sectional genus
nodes.statement: Let $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ be an integral and non-degenerate surface of sectional genus $g$ and degree $d$. Then $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _{X}(2)) \le \binom{n+1}{2} - 2d-1+g$. \begin{proof} Let $H\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ be a general hyperplane. Consider the exact sequence \begin{equation} 0 \longrightarrow \enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)\longrightarrow \enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)\longrightarrow \enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(s)\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} Since $H$ is general, $C = X\cap H$ is a smooth curve of degree $d$ and genus $g$. Hence, by Riemann-Roch, $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}}_C(2)) \geq 2d+1-g$. Thus \[ h^0(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(2)) \le \binom{n+1}{2} - 2d-1+g. \] By (\ref{eqw1}) and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(1)) =0$, the conclusion follows. \end{proof}
assumptions: $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ be an integral and non-degenerate surface of sectional genus $g$ and degree $d$
nodes.label: w2

nodes.name: Proof of Remark 4.7
nodes.statement: Let $H\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ be a general hyperplane. Consider the exact sequence \begin{equation} 0 \longrightarrow \enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)\longrightarrow \enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)\longrightarrow \enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(s)\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} Since $H$ is general, $C = X\cap H$ is a smooth curve of degree $d$ and genus $g$. Hence, by Riemann-Roch, $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}}_C(2)) \geq 2d+1-g$. Thus \[ h^0(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(2)) \le \binom{n+1}{2} - 2d-1+g. \] By (\ref{eqw1}) and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(1)) =0$, the conclusion follows.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to a general hyperplane section curve and apply Riemann-Roch with the sequence (4).

nodes.name: Hyperplane exact sequence (4)
nodes.statement: 0 \longrightarrow \enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)\longrightarrow \enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)\longrightarrow \enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(s)\longrightarrow 0.
nodes.label: eqw1

nodes.name: Hyperplane sequence
nodes.statement: Let $H\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ be a general hyperplane. Consider the exact sequence \begin{equation} 0 \longrightarrow \enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)\longrightarrow \enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)\longrightarrow \enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(s)\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Take a general hyperplane and its restriction sequence (4).

nodes.name: Riemann-Roch on C
nodes.statement: Since $H$ is general, $C = X\cap H$ is a smooth curve of degree $d$ and genus $g$. Hence, by Riemann-Roch, $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}}_C(2)) \geq 2d+1-g$.
nodes.statement_short: The section C is a smooth curve; Riemann-Roch bounds h^0(O_C(2)).

nodes.name: Bound on H
nodes.statement: Thus \[ h^0(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(2)) \le \binom{n+1}{2} - 2d-1+g. \]
nodes.statement_short: Bound quadrics in H through C.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: By (\ref{eqw1}) and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(1)) =0$, the conclusion follows.
nodes.statement_short: Lift the bound via (4).

nodes.name: Surfaces of almost-minimal degree
nodes.statement: A complete classification of surfaces of almost-minimal degree, i.e., all integral and non-degenerate surfaces $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ such that $\deg (X) =n$ is known; see, e.g., \cite{hsv, park1}. Let $H\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ be a general hyperplane. Since $C=X\cap H$ is a degree $n$ integral curve spanning $H$, there are two possibilities: either $C$ is arithmetically Cohen-Macaulay with $p_a(C) =1$ or $C$ is a smooth rational curve. In the latter case, $X$ may have only finitely many singular points. \begin{enumerate} \item[(i)] $C$ is arithmetically Cohen-Macaulay with $p_a({C}) =1$. The surface $X$ is linearly normal of degree $\deg(X)\geq 2p_a(C)+1$. Note that this case may occur for all $n$: take a cone over a linearly normal elliptic curve $C\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}$. \vspace{3mm} \item[(ii)] $C$ is a smooth rational curve. Thus $h^1(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(1)) =1$, $h^1(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(2)) =0$, and so $h^0(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(2)) = \binom{n+1}{2} -2n-1$. It is clear that \[ h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(1)) \le h^1(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(1)) =1. \] From (\ref{eqw1}), we derive $\binom{n+1}{2} -2n-2\le h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(2)) \le \binom{n+1}{2} -2n-1$. Now, if $X$ is smooth and $X\cap H$ is rational, then the classification of surfaces gives that $X$ is rational. Thus $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X)=0$. A standard exact sequence gives $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(1)) =h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _{X\cap H}(1)) +1=n+2$ and $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(2))= h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _{X\cap H}(2)) +h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(1)) = 3n+3$. Thus $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(1)) =1$ and so $X$ is not linearly normal. Let $X'\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^{n+1}$ be a smooth surface such that $X$ is an isomorphic linear projection of $X'$ from some $p\in \enm{\mathbb{P}}^{n+1}$ with $p$ not contained in the secant variety of $X'$. Thus $\deg(X') = n$ and since $X'\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^{n+1}$, it is either a minimal degree surface scroll or (when $n=4$) the Veronese surface. In any case, one knows the minimal free resolution of $X'$, and it follows that $X'$ has property $K_2$, following Alzati and Russo \cite[Definition 3.1]{ar}. By \cite[Theorem 3.2 or Corollary 3.3]{ar}, we have $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(2))=0$. Hence $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(2)) =\binom{n+2}{2} -3n-3$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Hyperplane sections of degree-n surfaces in P^n are elliptic ACM or smooth rational; in the rational case h^0(I_X(2)) is computed via Alzati-Russo.
